title: The book in hand

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gathering, everyone on one plain, and your line: all together. Did you look around a crowd once and remember? Today, on that plain, something is placed in each person's hand. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

A kid bursts out of the school gate on the last day of school, waving a report card over their head. Look! Read it! They can't wait for someone to see. The Qur'an has a moment with that same joy in it, on the Day of Resurrection. In Surah al-Haqqah, Pickthall's translation reads: "Then, as for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say: Take, read my book!" Take it, read it. Today, the book in hand.
screen: `A REPORT CARD, WAVED HIGH.` → `GIVEN IN THE RIGHT HAND.` → `TAKE, READ MY BOOK!`

segments.voice: The Qur'an speaks of a written record of each life, kitab, a book. Surah al-Infitar speaks of guardians, noble recorders, who know what people do. On the Day, the book is handed over. In the right hand, joy: take, read my book. In al-Haqqah, the next scene is the opposite. The one handed the book in the left hand says, in paraphrase: I wish I had never been given my book, I wish I had never known my reckoning. Same plain, same book, two faces. And who reads it? Surah al-Isra' answers, Pickthall again: "Read thy book. Thy soul sufficeth as reckoner against thee this day." No one else needs to read it out. You read your own. Surah al-Kahf adds one more line: those who see their books ask what kind of book this is, which leaves nothing out, small or great, but counts it. Small things. A tone of voice. A held door. Now, if that were the whole picture it would be frightening, and here a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari changes the arithmetic. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said that Allah wrote down good deeds and bad ones. Whoever intends a good deed and doesn't do it, one full good deed is written for them. If they do it, ten, up to seven hundred times, or more. Whoever intends a bad deed and holds back, that's written as a good deed. And if they do it, it's written as one. The book counts everything, and it counts generously. So the book is a record, not a trap: there is still time to write in it.
screen: `KITAB: A WRITTEN RECORD OF EACH LIFE.` · `RIGHT HAND, LEFT HAND.` · `READ THY BOOK.` · then, large: `IT COUNTS EVERYTHING, AND GENEROUSLY.`

segments.voice: The practice: do a deed for your record. Settle, and breathe. Find one good thing you've been meaning to do and haven't. Small is fine; al-Kahf says small things are counted. A visit you keep putting off. Returning something you borrowed. Taking out a neighbor's trash. Choose one. Now hold the intention clearly, because by the hadith, the intention alone is already written. Breathe with it. Then picture yourself actually doing it, today, in a particular place, at a particular time. If you pray, you can ask that it be accepted. The bell holds the time.
The book in hand. The record of each life, given in the right hand or the left on the Day, and read by its owner. Today's word.
Your line: the book of deeds. Today, do the deed you chose, and don't mention it to anyone. Let it go in the book quietly. Tomorrow, the scale. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims believe angels record each person's deeds and that the record will be given to them on the Day of Resurrection, in the right hand or the left; the hope to receive it in the right hand appears in prayers and sermons.

what a scholar hears: right hand and left in al-Haqqah, thy soul as reckoner in al-Isra', and the generous count in Bukhari: intentions written, good multiplied.

notes: Sahih al-Bukhari 6491: confirm number and the paraphrase (ten to seven hundred times or more; a bad deed held back is written as a good deed).
Hook: 'almost that exact picture' compares 69:19 to a child with a report card; confirm tone is respectful.

Editor pass: hook's 'almost that exact picture' softened; 'the line that unsettles people' (telling the listener's feeling) cut; practice no longer repeats day 1249's 'one small good thing you could do today' and its message example, and now starts from a deed already intended, tying to the intention hadith.
Noble recorders (82:10–12) are understood as angels; the script keeps to the Qur'an's wording.
